<problem>
For a nonempty finite poset $S$, a linear extension is a total order on its underlying set that extends its partial order. Its order dimension $\dim S$ is the least positive integer $t$ for which there are linear extensions $L_1,\ldots,L_t$ such that $x\le_S y$ if and only if $x\le_{L_i}y$ for every $i$.

For each positive integer $k$, write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Let $\lambda(k)$ be the number of inclusion-maximal intersecting families of subsets of $[k]$: a family $\mathcal F$ is intersecting when $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$ for all $A,B\in\mathcal F$, including $A=B$, and it is inclusion-maximal when no proper larger family of subsets of $[k]$ is intersecting.

Fix an integer $d\ge8$ and put $M_d=\lambda(d-1)+1$. Let $Q_d$ be the poset consisting of all one-element and two-element subsets of $[M_d]$, ordered by inclusion. For a nonempty finite poset $P$, order $P\times Q_d$ by $(p,A)\le(p',A')$ exactly when $p\le_P p'$ and $A\subseteq A'$.

Let $F(d)$ be the supremum of $\dim(P\times Q_d)-\dim P$ as $P$ ranges over all nonempty finite posets with $\dim P\ge3$. Determine $F(d)$ exactly for every integer $d\ge8$.
</problem>

17	## 1. The dimension lower bound

21	### Lemma 1

23	
24	**Proof.**

26	\[
27	S(a,b)=\{j:a\text{ follows }b\text{ in permutation }j\}.
28	\]

30	\[
31	S(a,b)\cap S(a,c)\ne\varnothing.
32	\]
33	The sets \(S(a,b)\), for fixed \(a\), therefore form an intersecting family, which can be extended to a maximal intersecting family \(\mathcal F_a\) on \([r]\).

52	## 2. The permutation construction needed for products
53	
54	A **three-labelled permutation system** on a set \(V\) consists of permutations
55	\[
56	R_1,\ldots,R_r
57	\]
58	and labels \(c_j(v)\in\{1,2,3\}\), satisfying:
59	
60	* **Triple property:** for distinct \(a,b,c\), some \(R_j\) puts \(a\) after both \(b,c\).
61	* **Labelled pair property:** for \(a\ne b\) and each \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\), some \(R_j\) puts \(a\) after \(b\) and has \(c_j(a)=i\).
62	
63	Labels may depend on both the row and the element.
64	
65	### Lemma 2
66	If such a system exists on \(n\) elements with \(r\) permutations, then
67	\[
68	\dim(P\times Q(n))\le \dim P+r-3
69	\]
70	whenever \(\dim P\ge3\).
71	
72	**Proof.**
73	Let \(L_1,\ldots,L_t\) realize \(P\).
74	
75	For each \(R_j\), assign \(A\in Q(n)\) to the block of its last element \(v\) in \(R_j\). Order the product by:
76	
77	1. the blocks, in order \(R_j\);
78	2. within block \(v\), the \(P\)-coordinate in \(L_{c_j(v)}\);
79	3. within a fixed \(P\)-coordinate and block, the singleton before the doubletons, with arbitrary tie-breaking.
80	
81	This is a linear extension. Add \(t-3\) \(P\)-priority lexicographic extensions, using \(L_4,\ldots,L_t\).
82	
83	Consider \((p,A)\not\le(p',B)\).
84	
85	If \(A\nsubseteq B\), choose \(a\in A\setminus B\). The triple property, or the labelled pair property when \(|B|=1\), gives a row putting \(a\) after every element of \(B\). Thus the block of \(A\) follows the block of \(B\).
86	
87	Otherwise \(A\subseteq B\) and \(p\not\le p'\). Choose \(L_i\) putting \(p\) after \(p'\). If \(i\ge4\), its \(P\)-priority extension works. If \(i\le3\), the labelled pair property supplies a row in which \(A,B\) have the same block, labelled \(i\):
88	
89	* if \(B=\{a,b\}\), choose \(a\in A\) and put \(a\) after \(b\) with label \(i\);
90	* if \(B=\{a\}\), choose any other element to obtain a row labelling \(a\) by \(i\).
91	
92	The within-block order then reverses the required pair. ∎
93	
94	We will construct a system with
95	\[
96	r=d,\qquad |V|\ge\lambda(d-1)+1.
97	\tag{4}
98	\]
99	
100	---

102	## 3. A source of labelled permutation systems
103	
104	Partition \([r]\) into three nonempty groups \(G_1,G_2,G_3\), and put
105	\[
106	\mathcal R=\{X\subseteq[r]:0<|X\cap G_i|<|G_i|\text{ for }i=1,2,3\}.
107	\]
108	This is a complement-closed inclusion poset.
109	
110	Call an upset \(\mathcal U\) of \(\mathcal R\) **self-dual** if exactly one of \(X,X^c\) belongs to \(\mathcal U\), for every \(X\in\mathcal R\). Let \(h(G_1,G_2,G_3)\) count these upsets.
111	
112	Every such \(\mathcal U\) is intersecting: if \(X,Y\in\mathcal U\) were disjoint, then \(X\subseteq Y^c\), forcing \(Y^c\in\mathcal U\).
113	
114	### Lemma 3
115	There is a three-labelled permutation system on
116	\[
117	h(G_1,G_2,G_3)
118	\]
119	elements, with \(r\) permutations and constant row labels \(c_j=i\) for \(j\in G_i\).
120	
121	**Proof.**
122	The elements are the self-dual upsets. Fix a priority order on the features \(X\in\mathcal R\). For each \(j\in[r]\), lexicographically order their membership vectors, preferring membership \(1\) later if \(j\in X\), and membership \(0\) later if \(j\notin X\).
123	
124	For distinct \(\mathcal U,\mathcal W\), let \(X\) be their first differing feature. The set of rows putting \(\mathcal U\) after \(\mathcal W\) is
125	\[
126	S(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)=
127	\begin{cases}
128	X,&X\in\mathcal U,\\
129	X^c,&X\notin\mathcal U.
130	\end{cases}
131	\]
132	It belongs to \(\mathcal U\) and to \(\mathcal R\). It therefore meets each \(G_i\), proving the labelled pair property. Two such comparison sets for a fixed \(\mathcal U\) intersect, proving the triple property. ∎
133	
134	We next count enough self-dual upsets.
135	
136	### Even \(r=2m\)
137	
138	Let \(W\) be the number of members of \(\mathcal R\) of size \(m\). Include all larger members, exclude all smaller members, and choose one member of each complementary pair at size \(m\). This gives
139	\[
140	h(G_1,G_2,G_3)\ge 2^{W/2}.
141	\tag{5}
142	\]
143	
144	### Odd \(r=2m+1\)
145	
146	Let \(\mathcal H\) be any intersecting subfamily of
147	\[
148	\mathcal R_m=\{X\in\mathcal R:|X|=m\}.
149	\]
150	Use \(\mathcal H\) at level \(m\), its self-dual completion at level \(m+1\), include everything above, and exclude everything below. This is a self-dual upset.
151	
152	In particular, if
153	\[
154	\mathcal S_j=\{X\in\mathcal R_m:j\in X\},
155	\]
156	then
157	\[
158	h(G_1,G_2,G_3)\ge 2^{|\mathcal S_j|}.
159	\tag{6}
160	\]
161	Unions of the power sets of several stars give stronger bounds when needed.
162

165	## 4. Bounds on Boolean upsets
166	
167	Let \(D(q)\) count all upsets of \(2^{[q]}\), and \(I(q)\) count the intersecting upsets.
168	
169	We need
170	\[
171	\lambda(q+1)=I(q)\le D(q).
172	\tag{7}
173	\]
174	To prove the identity, a maximal intersecting family on \([q+1]\) restricts to an intersecting upset \(\mathcal H\) on \([q]\). Conversely, \(\mathcal H\) determines the maximal intersecting family
175	\[
176	\mathcal H\ \cup\
177	\{A\cup\{q+1\}:[q]\setminus A\notin\mathcal H\}.
178	\]
179	These operations are inverse.
180	
181	Also,
182	\[
183	D(q+1)\le D(q)^2,
184	\tag{8}
185	\]
186	by restricting an upset according to the last coordinate.
187	
188	We use the following elementary bound:
189	\[
190	D(q)\le 3^{\binom q{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}}.
191	\tag{9}
192	\]
193	
194	Here is a proof, included to avoid using an asymptotic estimate. There is an ordered symmetric-chain decomposition of the Boolean lattice with this property:
195	
196	> For every three consecutive elements \(x<y<z\) of a chain, the other element strictly between \(x,z\) lies in an earlier chain.
197	
198	Construct it recursively. From an ordered chain \(C=(x_0,\ldots,x_{\ell-1})\), append, in this order,
199	\[
200	(x_0\cup\{q+1\},\ldots,x_{\ell-2}\cup\{q+1\})
201	\]
202	if nonempty, and
203	\[
204	(x_0,\ldots,x_{\ell-1},x_{\ell-1}\cup\{q+1\}).
205	\]
206	The property follows inductively; the final triple in the second chain uses an element of the first chain.
207	
208	Reveal an upset chain by chain in this order. Its unforced values on the next chain form an interval. There cannot be three consecutive unforced values, because the already-revealed alternate midpoint would force one endpoint. Thus there are at most two unforced values, and at most three possible patterns. A symmetric-chain decomposition has \(\binom q{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}\) chains, proving (9).

212	## 5. Constructing the systems for all \(d\ge8\)
213	
214	### 5.1. The case \(d=8\)
215	
216	For group sizes \(2,3,3\),
217	\[
218	h(2,3,3)=783558.
219	\tag{10}
220	\]
221	This finite count is derived and computed below.
222	
223	Take two copies of this system on \(N=783558\) elements. Put
224	\[

226	\]

344	## 6. The finite counts and executable verification

346	Here is why the four enumerations used above are finite counting proofs.

348	* Intersecting upsets of \(2^{[q]}\) correspond to intersecting antichains of nonempty subsets, via their minimal members. These are independent sets in the graph joining comparable or disjoint subsets. The code counts them by

347	## 4. Bounds on Boolean upsets
348	
349	Let \(D(q)\) count all upsets of \(2^{[q]}\), and \(I(q)\) count the intersecting upsets.
350	
351	We need
352	\[
353	\lambda(q+1)=I(q)\le D(q).
354	\tag{7}
355	\]
356	To prove the identity, a maximal intersecting family on \([q+1]\) restricts to an intersecting upset \(\mathcal H\) on \([q]\). Conversely, \(\mathcal H\) determines the maximal intersecting family
357	\[
358	\mathcal H\ \cup\
359	\{A\cup\{q+1\}:[q]\setminus A\notin\mathcal H\}.
360	\]
361	These operations are inverse.
362	
363	Also,
364	\[
365	D(q+1)\le D(q)^2,
366	\tag{8}
367	\]
368	by restricting an upset according to the last coordinate.
369	
370	We use the following elementary bound:
371	\[
372	D(q)\le 3^{\binom q{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}}.
373	\tag{9}
374	\]
375	
376	Here is a proof, included to avoid using an asymptotic estimate. There is an ordered symmetric-chain decomposition of the Boolean lattice with this property:
377	
378	> For every three consecutive elements \(x<y<z\) of a chain, the other element strictly between \(x,z\) lies in an earlier chain.
379	
380	Construct it recursively. From an ordered chain \(C=(x_0,\ldots,x_{\ell-1})\), append, in this order,
381	\[
382	(x_0\cup\{q+1\},\ldots,x_{\ell-2}\cup\{q+1\})
383	\]
384	if nonempty, and
385	\[
386	(x_0,\ldots,x_{\ell-1},x_{\ell-1}\cup\{q+1\}).
387	\]
388	The property follows inductively; the final triple in the second chain uses an element of the first chain.
389	
390	Reveal an upset chain by chain in this order. Its unforced values on the next chain form an interval. There cannot be three consecutive unforced values, because the already-revealed alternate midpoint would force one endpoint. Thus there are at most two unforced values, and at most three possible patterns. A symmetric-chain decomposition has \(\binom q{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}\) chains, proving (9).

530	* Intersecting upsets of \(2^{[q]}\) correspond to intersecting antichains of nonempty subsets, via their minimal members. These are independent sets in the graph joining comparable or disjoint subsets. The code counts them by
531	  \[
532	  f(M)=f(M\setminus\{v\})+f(M\setminus N[v]).

536	* Let \(S\) be the six-element poset of proper nonempty subsets of \([3]\). If \(J(T)\) is the set of ideals of \(T\), define
537	  \[
538	  C_{AB}=|\{K\in J(T):K\subseteq A\cap B\}|.
539	  \]
540	  Choosing the three ideals at the lower elements of \(S\), and then the three upper ideals, shows
541	  \[
542	  |J(S\times T)|=\operatorname{tr}(C^3).
543	  \tag{15}
544	  \]
